Text is in our own words at about a 3rd-grade reading level. Worldwide wording: say cold season, not month names. Metric first. Facts checked against the cited extension pages. guides.blurb: Help honey bees get through the cold season. Do the mite and food work early, before nights stay cold. Moisture and mites hurt more hives than the cold itself.
intro: These steps are for honey bee hives. Wild bees spend the cold season in other ways — leave some healthy hollow stems for them if you can (see the garden checklist).
Start this work well before the first frost, especially mite checks and feeding. Always follow the label on any mite treatment.

climate.text: Bees may stay in a tight cluster for many weeks and cannot fly often. Plan on about 18–27 kg (40–60 lb) of honey stores. A windbreak and a wrap are often used. A small upper opening is very important so moist air can leave.

Bees may fly on many winter days. They need less stored honey than in a cold place, but you should still check the weight and feed if the hive feels light. Wrapping is often not needed at low elevations. You may still want a smaller door, a mouse guard, and a way for moist air to leave.

items.t: Check stores and feed if the hive is light. In a cold climate, many hives need about 18–27 kg (40–60 lb) of honey. Mild climates need less. Food should sit above the bees, because the cluster moves up.

Test for Varroa mites and treat if needed before the cold season, while treatments still work. Follow the product label. A second treatment with a different product may be needed later — only as the label allows.
Fit a mouse guard on the lower door. Use mesh about 1 cm (3/8 in) wide so bees can pass but mice cannot.
Give the hive a small upper opening so moist air can leave. Wet bees get cold and can die. Bees handle dry cold better than drips from the lid.
Tilt the hive a little toward the front so any water can run out the door.
Put a windbreak on the windy side, or set the hive where the wind is weaker. Face the door away from the strongest wind if you can.
In a cold climate, wrap or insulate the hive if that is common where you live. Do not block the top or bottom openings. In a mild climate, wrapping is often not needed.
Make the lower door smaller so less cold wind gets in and fewer robber bees can enter.
Weigh down the outer cover so a storm cannot blow it off. Strap the boxes together if winter winds are strong.
Keep the hive off the damp ground on a stand.
On a mild day in the cold season, heft the hive. If it feels light, add sugar feed. Do not break the winter cluster in deep cold.

lessons: Varroa mites and how to count them

guides.blurb: Tuck the garden in for the cold season: clean up sick plants, protect soil and perennials, and drain water lines so they do not freeze and split.
intro: You do not need to strip the garden bare. Take away sick plants, but you can leave some healthy stems and leaves for wild bees and for the soil.
The lessons and project guides below already cover mulch, cover crops, frost cloth, and pots. Use this list so you do not miss a step.

climate.text: Drain hoses and irrigation before a hard freeze. Mulch perennials after the soil starts to freeze, so plants do not think it is time to grow. Have frost cloth ready for early cold nights.
Hard freezes may be rare, but a sudden cold night can still hurt tender plants. Keep frost cloth handy. You may still grow in the cool season. Drain hoses if nights can drop below freezing.

items.t: Pull out sick plants (blight, mildew, and the like) and put them in the trash, not in the compost, so the disease does not come back.
Leave some healthy hollow stems and a few seed heads if you can. Wild bees and other helpful insects use them in the cold season.
Pick tender crops before a hard frost. Root crops can often stay in the ground a little longer. See the lesson on saving green tomatoes.
Cover bare soil with about 5–8 cm (2–3 in) of mulch. For perennials, wait until the soil starts to freeze, and keep mulch a little away from stems and crowns.
Sow a cover crop on empty beds while the soil is still warm enough for seeds to sprout. The plants hold the soil and feed it later.
Protect tender perennials: mulch, wrap, or move pots to a safer place. See the lessons on pots in winter, figs, and storing dahlia tubers.
Have frost cloth ready. Cover tender plants on frosty nights, and take the cloth off when the day warms.
Disconnect and drain hoses, drip lines, and outdoor taps so leftover water cannot freeze and split them. Store hoses dry.
If the soil is dry, water trees and shrubs until the ground freezes. Moist soil is kinder to roots than dry soil in the cold.

lessons: Mulch is a blanket for soil
Tuck plants in on a frosty night
Why potted plants die in winter
Help a fig tree live through a cold winter

guides.blurb: Get a greenhouse or hoop house ready for the cold season: more insulation, safe heat, vents that still open, and a frame that can take snow.
intro: A greenhouse can get too hot on a sunny winter day and too wet or too cold at night. Plan for both.
The greenhouse and weather lessons already in the app explain how air, heat, and snow work. This list is the seasonal check.

climate.text: Insulation (such as greenhouse bubble wrap on the inside) helps hold heat. Brush off heavy snow. Use only a heater made for this kind of space, and give a fuel heater fresh air plus a carbon monoxide alarm.
You may not need extra heat most nights, but you still need vents that open on bright days. Check the cover after wind and rain. A sudden cold snap can still harm tender plants.

items.t: Wash the walls and roof so more light can get in. Check for cracks, holes, and loose clips, and fix them.
In a cold climate, add clear greenhouse bubble wrap or another safe insulation on the inside. Leave vents and doors free to open. Do not cover heaters or flues.

If you use heat, use a heater made for greenhouses or that indoor space. Keep it away from plants and plastic. For a fuel heater, give it fresh air and use a carbon monoxide alarm. Never use a camping stove or a heater that is not safe indoors.
Make sure vents or roll-up sides can still open on sunny days so plants do not cook, even in the cool season.
Know how much snow your frame can hold. A peaked roof sheds snow better than a round one. Brush off heavy, wet snow and check the frame after storms.
Seal gaps that waste heat, but do not make the house so tight that moist air cannot leave.
Plan a water source that will not freeze, or bring water in as you need it. Drain lines that could freeze.
If vents or heat need electricity, have a plan if the power goes out.

lessons: Greenhouse air: letting heat out and keeping it in
Stretch the season: row covers and cold frames

guides.blurb: Get sheds, tool stores, and root cellars ready: care for tools, keep rodents out, drain fuel and water, and store chemicals where they will not freeze.
intro: A dry, tight shed and clean tools save work next season. The tool-care lessons and project guide already show how to clean, oil, and sharpen.
If you keep food in a root cellar, check that it stays cool, a little moist, and closed to mice.

climate.text: Liquids and many garden chemicals can be ruined if they freeze. Move them to a frost-free, locked, dry place. Drain engines, pumps, and hoses. Check the roof before snow piles up.
Hard freezes may be rare, but damp and mice are still a problem. Drain tools if a freeze is possible. Keep chemicals locked, dry, and out of strong sun.

items.t: Clean, dry, sharpen, and oil tools before you put them away. Hang or rack them so they stay dry.
Close holes where mice and rats can get in. Store seed, pet food, and produce in tight bins.
Drain fuel from mowers and other engines, or add fuel stabilizer and run the engine a short time, as the tool book says. Drain water from pumps and hoses.

Move garden chemicals and other liquids that can freeze to a frost-free, locked, dry place, away from children and pets. Keep them in the original labeled containers. Do not let them freeze or get very hot.
Check the roof, gutters, and walls of sheds. Fix leaks before a wet or snowy season. Latch or weigh doors so wind cannot blow them open.
If you have a root cellar, check that it stays cool and a little moist, that bins are clean, and that rodents cannot get in. See Preserve & Store for cellar guidance.

lessons: Store tools for the off season
